claims.text: The target materials are single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys such as CrCoNi.
Temperatures from 600°C to 1000°C are representative of high-temperature fusion-reactor environments.
High-temperature plastic strain and toughness are governed by synergy between intrinsic plasticity and extrinsic crack-shielding mechanisms.
Low average stacking-fault energy, potentially with local SFE variation, modulates the behavior of full and partial dislocations.
High lattice friction strengthens the alloy by increasing resistance to planar dislocation slip and influencing partial-dislocation motion.
Low SFE promotes the formation of nanoscale crack bridges within a few hundred nanometres of a crack tip.
Nanoscale crack bridges provide an extrinsic shielding contribution to toughness.
The combined low-SFE, high-lattice-friction, and crack-bridging mechanisms produce excellent strength, ductility, and toughness.
Temperature, strain rate, and alloy composition affect deformation behavior in HEAs.
Changing composition through additions such as Ta and W can be used to test effects on plastic strain and toughness.
Temperature, strain rate, and composition can be varied in a controlled experiment to test the proposed mechanism.
Optimizing composition and microstructure to obtain low average SFE, high lattice friction, and nanoscale crack bridging will enhance high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
The optimized HEA will outperform conventional alloys and HEAs without optimized composition and microstructure.
The hypothesis is limited to high-temperature conditions and depends on material composition and microstructure.
Grain size and impurities may also affect the mechanical properties.
Failure to enhance high-temperature plastic strain and toughness after achieving the specified low-SFE, high-friction, crack-bridging state would falsify the hypothesis.
